claims.claim: The United States operates parallel federal and state court systems, commonly called the dual court system; state courts hear most criminal cases and are the final interpreters of their own state's law, while federal courts hear constitutional questions, cases under federal statutes and treaties, admiralty, bankruptcy, disputes between states, and habeas corpus.

Congress has established 94 federal judicial districts, each with a U.S. district court and with at least one district court in each state and the District of Columbia, and 13 U.S. courts of appeals that sit below the Supreme Court. The Administrative Office also counts 90 U.S. bankruptcy courts, and each district includes a bankruptcy court as a unit of the district court.

The 94 district courts are organized into 12 regional circuits, each with its own court of appeals; the 13th court of appeals, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, has nationwide jurisdiction over specialized cases including patent cases and appeals from the U.S. Court of International Trade and the U.S. Court of Federal Claims.

Federal appellate courts do not retry cases, hear new evidence, or hear witnesses, and they use no jury; circuit judges usually sit in panels of three to determine whether the law was applied correctly.

Article III, Section 1 provides that the judges of the supreme and inferior courts hold their offices during good behaviour and receive compensation that may not be diminished during their continuance in office; federal judges are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate and may be removed only by congressional impeachment.

Not every federal judicial officer has life tenure. Under 28 U.S.C. 631 the district judges themselves appoint United States magistrate judges to eight-year full-time or four-year part-time terms; under 28 U.S.C. 152 the court of appeals for each circuit appoints bankruptcy judges to fourteen-year terms; and district judges in the territorial districts of Guam, the Virgin Islands, and the Northern Mariana Islands serve ten-year terms rather than serving during good behaviour.

A magistrate judge is a judicial officer of a district court who conducts initial proceedings in criminal cases, decides criminal misdemeanor cases, and handles many pretrial civil and criminal matters on behalf of district judges.

Article III, Section 2 gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction in cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, and those in which a state is a party, and appellate jurisdiction in the other enumerated cases, subject to such exceptions and regulations as Congress makes. Under 28 U.S.C. 1254, cases in the courts of appeals reach the Supreme Court by writ of certiorari granted on the petition of any party to any civil or criminal case, or by certification of a question of law by the court of appeals.

The Supreme Court's docket is discretionary and small relative to demand. The Court states that approximately 5,000 to 7,000 new cases are filed each Term, that plenary review with oral argument is currently granted in about 80 of them, and that it typically disposes of about 100 or more cases without plenary review; each week the Justices evaluate approximately 130 petitions seeking review of judgments of state and federal courts. Under the Rule of Four, four of the nine Justices must vote to accept a case, and the Court usually is not under any obligation to hear a case.

State court systems vary, but the common pattern is one or more levels of trial court, with courts of limited jurisdiction handling violations, infractions, and minor misdemeanors and courts of general jurisdiction handling felonies and major misdemeanors; most but not all states have intermediate appellate courts, and every state has a court of last resort, generally called the supreme court.

Court names do not travel between states. New York's Unified Court System criminal court structure chart places the Court of Appeals at the top; the Appellate Divisions of the Supreme Court, the Appellate Terms of the Supreme Court for the First and Second Departments, and the County Courts at the intermediate appellate level; and the Supreme Courts, County Courts, District Courts, New York City Criminal Courts, City Courts, Town Courts, and Village Courts among the courts of original instance. In New York the Supreme Court is a trial court and the County Courts appear at two levels at once.

Jurisdiction is the legal authority of a court to hear and decide a certain type of case. It is divided along several axes: the function of the court (trial courts resolve facts, appellate courts review the record for legal error), the subject matter of the case, the seriousness of the case (limited versus general jurisdiction), the court's authority over the parties, and geography under federalism.

Under 18 U.S.C. 3231 the district courts of the United States have original jurisdiction, exclusive of the courts of the states, of all offenses against the laws of the United States, and nothing in title 18 takes away or impairs the jurisdiction of the courts of the several states under their own laws.

In Gamble v. United States, No. 17-646, argued December 6, 2018 and decided June 17, 2019, the Supreme Court declined to overturn the dual-sovereignty doctrine, under which two offenses are not the same offence for double jeopardy purposes if they are prosecuted by different sovereigns. Gamble pleaded guilty to violating Alabama's felon-in-possession statute and was then indicted federally for the same instance of possession; the Eleventh Circuit's judgment was affirmed. Justice Alito wrote for the Court, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Thomas, Breyer, Sotomayor, Kagan, and Kavanaugh; Justices Ginsburg and Gorsuch each filed a dissent. The syllabus also records the Court's observation that eliminating the dual-sovereignty rule would do little to trim the reach of federal criminal law or prevent many successive state and federal prosecutions for the same criminal conduct.

The courtroom workgroup is a standard framework in criminal courts scholarship for explaining decision patterns and dynamics in criminal trial courts in common law jurisdictions, and it treats the relationships among the judges and lawyers who appear together repeatedly as interdependent rather than purely adversarial.

The book most often associated with the courtroom workgroup framework is James Eisenstein and Herbert Jacob, Felony Justice: An Organizational Analysis of Criminal Courts, first published by Little, Brown in 1977.
claims.status: partially-supported: the bibliographic record (title, subtitle, authors, 1977, publisher) is verified from the Open Library catalog record; the lesson does not claim the book originated the term, only that it is the study usually named alongside the framework

claims.claim: Methods of selecting state judges vary by state and include election, appointment for a given number of years, appointment for life, and combinations such as appointment followed by election.

Missouri's Nonpartisan Selection of Judges Court Plan, adopted by constitutional amendment in November 1940 and the model for merit selection elsewhere, works by having a judicial commission review applications, interview candidates, and submit three names to the governor; if the governor does not appoint one of the three within 60 days, the commission selects one. A judge who has served at least one year must then stand for a retention election at the next general election on a separate nonpartisan judicial ballot and must receive a majority to be retained.

The Bureau of Justice Statistics counted 3,052 problem-solving courts in the United States in 2012, the most common types being drug courts (1,330, or 44%) and mental health courts (337, or 11%). Sixty-five percent accepted cases after the defendant entered a guilty plea, participants spent a median of one year in the program, and successful completion commonly meant dismissal of the case (61%) or a suspended sentence (40%).

The National Institute of Justice's CrimeSolutions clearinghouse rated the practice of adult drug courts Promising for the crime and delinquency outcomes covering multiple crime/offense types and drug and alcohol offenses, and Ineffective for the drugs and substance abuse outcome covering multiple substances, in a profile posted September 9, 2013 that the site marks as no longer updated.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many cases the Supreme Court reviews and how many petitions it receives
positions: The Supreme Court's own Supreme Court at Work page: approximately 5,000-7,000 new cases filed each Term, plenary review with oral argument granted in about 80, about 100 or more disposed of without plenary review.
The federal judiciary's Supreme Court Procedures educational page: the Court accepts 100-150 of the more than 7,000 cases it is asked to review each year.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are official and they are not measuring quite the same thing: the Court's own page separates plenary review from summary disposition, while the educational page combines them and rounds the filing total upward. The lesson reports the Court's own figures for its docket and uses the educational page only for the Rule of Four and for the original/appellate definitions, and it states that both are approximations rather than a fixed annual count.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the count of problem-solving courts is current
positions: BJS's Census of Problem-Solving Courts counted 3,052 courts as of 2012 and was published in September 2016.
No comparable national census has been published since.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson dates the figure explicitly as a 2012 count published in 2016 and does not present it as a current number.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether every state has an intermediate appellate court
positions: The Administrative Office describes state systems as typically having a supreme court, intermediate appellate courts, and trial courts.
The open textbook states that most states have intermediate courts of appeals and that some have more than one level of them.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says most states have an intermediate appellate level and that some do not, rather than asserting a count of states without one, because no source consulted in this session gave a current, dated state-by-state tally.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no verifiable content about courts at all: it described 'court structure' as a generic organizing concept, offered a toolbox-drawer analogy, and asserted nothing about the federal or state judiciaries, jurisdiction, or judicial selection.
The draft's vocabulary list defined 'Court Structure' circularly as 'a foundational Criminal Justice & Criminology concept covered in this lesson', which asserts nothing checkable.
The draft's three quick-check questions tested only the generic idea that concepts should be applied with context, not any fact about courts.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft with researched content on the dual court system, federal and state hierarchies, jurisdiction, dual sovereignty, the courtroom workgroup, judicial selection, and problem-solving courts.

Verified the counts of 94 district courts and 13 courts of appeals against the Administrative Office rather than reusing them from memory, and added the 12-regional-circuits-plus-Federal-Circuit breakdown the sibling merged topic did not carry.
Verified Gamble v. United States by reading the slip opinion syllabus and lineup rather than a case summary, including the docket number, argument and decision dates, and the 7-2 division.
Recorded the Supreme Court's own docket figures rather than the higher, rounder numbers on the judiciary's educational page, and flagged the discrepancy.

Dated the problem-solving court count to the 2012 census and reported the drug court evidence at the strength CrimeSolutions actually assigned, including the no-effects rating for substance use outcomes.

Dropped judicialselection.us, which appears in older reference lists as a National Center for State Courts project: the domain now serves unrelated commercial gambling content and was not used for anything.
rightsIssues: Federal judiciary and Supreme Court web pages are recorded REFERENCE_ONLY: they are U.S. government works but carry no explicit reuse grant on the page, so no wording from them was adapted.
Statutory text from uscode.house.gov and the text of the Constitution are U.S. government edicts in the public domain; two short statutory phrases are quoted with attribution.
The Gamble slip opinion is a public-domain federal judicial opinion; the syllabus was read for facts, holding, and lineup, and no passage longer than a short phrase is reproduced.

The SOU-CCJ230 open textbook chapters used here are Copyright 2019 Lore Rutz-Burri under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, not the CC BY-SA license the book's front matter shows. Because the NonCommercial term could conflict with downstream use, these chapters are recorded REFERENCE_ONLY and no prose or structure was adapted from them.

The New York court structure chart is a New York State Unified Court System page image; the live host blocks automated retrieval, so it was read through an Internet Archive capture. Recorded REFERENCE_ONLY, described in original words, not reproduced.
The Missouri Judiciary page was likewise read through an Internet Archive capture and is recorded REFERENCE_ONLY.
Young (2013) is a paywalled journal article; only the publisher-supplied abstract retrieved through the Crossref API was read, and the lesson's use of it is limited to what that abstract states.
Open Library catalog data is CC0-dedicated bibliographic metadata and is used only to verify authors, title, subtitle, year, and publisher.
